Let me begin the discussion by pitching into the industry landscape initially, post which 
I will discuss Rallis' specific developments.  
Domestic Market: India’s agri-input sector faced significant headwinds during the 
2026 Kharif season amid deficient and erratic rainfall, crop-mix changes, subdued farm 
economics and heightened competitive intensity. Moisture stress across key 
agricultural states like Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Telangana, parts of 
Punjab and Haryana affected crop prospects for paddy, soybean, maize, cotton and 
pulses, weighing on demand for herbicides, fungicides, insecticides and seed-treatment 
products. Softer product prices, higher trade discounts and channel inventory pressures 
further constrained fresh purchases. Consequently, domestic demand recovery is likely 
to remain uneven, contingent on crop conditions, irrigation availability and a revival in 
farmer profitability.  
Global Markets, Commodity Prices & Industry Margins: Since April 2026, global 
agricultural markets have experienced firmer commodity prices amid weather-related 
supply risks and geopolitical disruptions. In September, the FAO Food Price Index rose 
1.5% month-on-month, while its cereal price index increased 5.1%, driven by higher 
wheat and maize prices amid Black Sea logistical disruptions and adverse weather 
conditions. Vegetable oil and sugar prices also strengthened on the back of import 
demand, weather concerns and production uncertainties across key producing regions. 
Although global cereal production is forecasted to decline 2.1% in 2026, the projected 
harvest remains the second largest on record, indicating tighter supply conditions rather 
than a widespread shortage. The Middle East crisis has heightened energy and freight 
costs, increasing pressure on agrochemical manufacturers’ input costs and margins. 
The firmer crop prices could support farm economics and agrochemical demand, the 
benefits may be offset by affordability constraints, competitive pricing and cautious 
channel replenishment, keeping the sector’s recovery uneven. 
The global agricultural sector is expected to expand over the medium term, supported 
by rising food demand, productivity improvements and agricultural intensification. The 
OECD–FAO projects global agricultural production value to increase by ~13% by 
2035, with Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America emerging as key growth 
regions. Latin America remains strategically important given its substantial soybean, 
maize and cotton acreage, while North America and Europe are mature, input-intensive 
markets. The global crop-protection market is estimated at ~US$70.4 billion in 2026, 
although growth will remain sensitive to farm economics, weather, regulation and 
product affordability.

For Indian exporters, favourable currency movements may support rupee realizations, 
but sustained volume recovery remains critical. International sales may also face 
pressure from subdued channel demand, distributor resistance, weather-related 
disruptions and heatwaves in Europe, which have affected crop conditions and input 
application patterns. For Indian companies, the key indicators to monitor are active-
ingredient and intermediate prices, freight rates, rupee movements, export order 
volumes, channel inventories and farmer affordability. Recent UN and international-
agency assessments also warn that prolonged shipping disruptions could affect crop 
yields and food prices into 2027. 
For the agrochemical industry, broadly firmer crop prices can improve farm economics 
and support demand for herbicides, insecticides and fungicides, particularly in export-
oriented agricultural regions. However, higher crude oil, energy, freight and input costs 
may put pressure on manufacturers’ margins, while elevated fertilizer costs could 
constrain farmers’ overall input spending. The outlook is therefore cautiously 
constructive: companies with strong distribution networks, differentiated products, 
efficient manufacturing and disciplined cost management are better positioned to 
benefit. A sustained recovery in agrochemical demand will ultimately depend on the 
persistence of higher crop prices, improved farm incomes and a recovery in channel 
inventory and purchasing activity. 
 
Rabi 2026–27 Outlook: The outlook remains sensitive to winter rainfall, soil moisture 
and irrigation availability. IMD’s northeast monsoon forecast of 88–112% of the long-
period average is relevant to southern peninsular India but does not guarantee adequate 
rainfall across the country. Major reservoirs held approximately 70% of capacity, 
below the 10-year average of 76.6%, with the southern region facing relatively greater 
irrigation concerns. These conditions could influence Rabi acreage, crop yields and 
farmer spending, particularly in water-stressed areas. The Government’s Rabi MSP 
increases for 2027–28 range from 0.97% for wheat to 10.32% for safflower, with 
mustard rising 6.66% and lentil 5.57%. While higher MSPs provide a measure of price 
support, actual farm returns will depend on yields, market prices and procurement. 
Moving to Rallis-specific developments: We had a muted Q2FY27 performance on 
the back of in-sufficient rainfall in the key agrochemical consuming states like Punjab, 
Haryana, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Telangana, etc. Our quarterly 
revenue stood at ₹ 858 cr versus ₹ 861 cr of Q2FY26. Overall, EBITDA for Q2FY27 
stood at ₹ 126 cr, lower by 18% compared to Q2 of the previous year. Profit after tax 
at ₹ 85 cr versus ₹ 102 cr of Q2FY26, which is 17% lower.  
 
Approximately 43% of India received ~19% deficient rains in comparison to the long 
period average this monsoon season, which delayed the kharif sowing. It resulted in 
slower liquidation and high carry-forward inventory. Due to prolonged geo-political 
situation, channel/farmers prioritized stocking for fertilizers rather than agro- 
chemicals. Fertilizers availability had been a concern due to logistics challenges.

alliances and farmer reach, and leveraging digitalization to enhance operational 
efficiency and drive sustainable growth.

H1FY27 PAT stood at ₹ 210 cr vs ₹ 197 cr of H1FY26, resulting in growth of 6%. 
We are focused on accelerating priority brand growth through sharper market 
execution, targeted product promotion and enhanced phygital (physical+digital)

priorities include strengthening the go-to-market strategy, expanding customer reach, 
optimizing the product portfolio and improving sales productivity through territory 
rationalization and cost efficiencies. Digital engagement, customer feedback and data-

In the Seeds segment, our primary focus will be on five strategic crops: Cotton, Maize, 
Millet, Mustard, and Rice. A selective and concentrated approach in these crops is

Overall, we remain disciplined in improving capital efficiency across both fixed capital 
and working capital. At quarter end our inventory levels remain elevated in comparison
